tEn: Ex-Twitter CEO Parag Agrawal's $2B Bet on Search for AI Agents
tZh: 前推特 CEO 帕拉格·阿格拉瓦尔的 20 亿美元押注：为 AI 智能体打造搜索
sEn: Parag Agrawal, former Twitter CEO and founder of Parallel, discusses his path from physics olympiad to Twitter leadership and his $2B bet on building search for AI agents.
sZh: 前推特 CEO、Parallel 创始人帕拉格·阿格拉瓦尔讲述从物理奥赛到执掌推特的历程，以及他 20 亿美元押注为 AI 智能体打造搜索的愿景。

consensus.en: Rapid change favors small, agile teams over incumbents with legacy constraints.
consensus.zh: 快速变化有利于小型敏捷团队，而非受遗留约束的现有巨头。

consensus.en: Agents will use the web 1000x more, requiring new search infrastructure built for agents.
consensus.zh: 智能体使用网络的频率将提升1000倍，需要为智能体构建新的搜索基础设施。

consensus.en: Agents need different search: longer inputs, token outputs, varied latency and compute budgets.
consensus.zh: 智能体需要不同的搜索：更长的输入、token输出、不同的延迟和算力预算。

consensus.en: The web must shift from pull to push, with proactive agents bringing relevant information.
consensus.zh: 网络必须从拉取转向推送，由主动的智能体带来相关信息。

consensus.en: Model capabilities will keep improving; the rate of change will remain high and disruptive.
consensus.zh: 模型能力将持续提升；变化速度将保持高位并具有颠覆性。

consensus.en: Leadership is about followership; adapt the company to yourself as CEO.
consensus.zh: 领导力在于追随者；作为CEO要让公司适应你，而非你适应公司。

contrarian.en: Google won't win agent search because its goal is to keep search for Google only.
contrarian.zh: 谷歌不会赢得智能体搜索，因为其目标是让搜索仅服务于谷歌。

contrarian.en: Labs like OpenAI and Anthropic won't own search; it's incidental to their model-centric mission.
contrarian.zh: OpenAI和Anthropic等实验室不会拥有搜索；搜索对其以模型为中心的使命是附带的。

contrarian.en: Walled gardens will be forced to open to agents, not remain closed, due to new incentive models.
contrarian.zh: 围墙花园将因新的激励模式被迫向智能体开放，而非保持封闭。

contrarian.en: Rushed AI regulation likely has unintended negative effects; burden of proof is on regulators.
contrarian.zh: 仓促的AI监管可能产生意外的负面效果；举证责任在监管者一方。

contrarian.en: Hiring for potential over experience is a non-scalable but effective way to build special teams.
contrarian.zh: hiring 潜力而非经验是一种不可扩展但有效的组建特殊团队的方式。

contrarian.en: AI gives CEOs more control by summarizing code and customer interactions, not information overload.
contrarian.zh: AI通过总结代码和客户互动给CEO更多控制力，而非信息过载。

turns.en: Google has the compute, the talent, the background, the index. Why isn't this Google's war to win?
turns.zh: 谷歌拥有算力、人才、背景和索引。为什么这不是谷歌的战争？

turns.en: I think you should invert the question. You had lawyers on almost every decision, knowing that this was looking like a contested moment. Credit to the leadership team there. Twitter continued operating well. We shipped a lot of valuable things in that period that I'm proud of. The deal isn't closed until it's closed. So you are now operating in this weird dual reality of we are committed to closing this deal and will put in every effort in the court of law to make sure it closes. And simultaneously, we are operating like it won't. I could keep these two contradictory things in my mind. It is very hard to have thousands of people operate in this sort of weird dual reality. Me, I'm in this camp of like the token maxxer camp. And then there is the responsible camp, which is like, oh, I need to build a reliable system in the presence of these token maxxers.
turns.zh: 我认为你应该反过来问这个问题。几乎每个决策都有律师参与，知道这看起来像是一个有争议的时刻。感谢那里的领导团队。Twitter 继续运营良好。我们在那个时期发布了许多有价值的东西，我为此感到自豪。交易在完成之前不算完成。所以你现在是在一个奇怪的双重现实中运作：我们致力于完成这笔交易，并将尽一切努力在法庭上确保它完成。同时，我们又像它不会完成一样运作。我可以在脑海中保持这两个矛盾的事情。很难让成千上万的人在这种奇怪的双重现实中运作。我属于代币最大化者阵营。然后是负责任阵营，他们觉得，哦，我需要在这些代币最大化者面前构建一个可靠的系统。

turns.en: Why be a founder at the age of 40?
turns.zh: 为什么在 40 岁时成为创始人？

turns.en: 40 is young. I only like jobs where I think that I am slightly unqualified for doing that.
turns.zh: 40 岁很年轻。我只喜欢那些我认为自己稍微不够格的工作。

turns.en: What are you unqualified for now? Parag Agrawal has been exceptional in almost everything he's done in his career. As a student, he was an international physics olympiad gold medalist, ranked in the top 100 in the IIT entrance exam, graduated at the top of his CS class at IIT Bombay, and then a Stanford PhD. He joined Twitter as a software engineer, rose to become the company's first distinguished engineer, then CTO, and eventually CEO, all within a decade. And today he's the founder of Parallel, a multi-billion dollar company backed by Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia. In this conversation, we talk about what drove him to excel in every aspect of his career, his mental models, his operating principles, and the internet of agencies building for. Nakul App. Parag, welcome to the show.
turns.zh: 你现在对什么不够格？帕拉格·阿格拉瓦尔在职业生涯中几乎每件事都表现出色。作为学生，他是国际物理奥林匹克金牌得主，在 IIT 入学考试中排名前 100，以计算机科学班级第一的成绩毕业于 IIT 孟买，然后获得斯坦福大学博士学位。他作为软件工程师加入 Twitter，在十年内晋升为该公司首位杰出工程师，然后成为 CTO，最终成为 CEO。如今，他是 Parallel 的创始人，这是一家由 Kleiner Perkins 和 Sequoia 支持的数十亿美元公司。在这次对话中，我们谈论了是什么驱动他在职业生涯的各个方面脱颖而出，他的心智模型，他的运营原则，以及他为代理构建的互联网。Nakul App。Parag，欢迎来到节目。

turns.en: Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请我。

turns.en: So, you know, before Twitter, before Parallel, you know, Physics Olympiad gold at 17 years of age, top of the CS class at IIT Bombay, Stanford PhD. So you really excelled in every aspect of your career. What were you as a kid? Like, were you always very ambitious and competitive?
turns.zh: 那么，你知道，在 Twitter 之前，在 Parallel 之前，你知道，17 岁时获得物理奥林匹克金牌，在 IIT 孟买计算机科学班级中名列前茅，斯坦福博士。所以你确实在职业生涯的每个方面都表现出色。你小时候是什么样的？比如，你一直都非常有野心和竞争力吗？

turns.en: I don't think people would have described me as ambitious. People would perhaps early on during middle school, high school would described me as happy go lucky. I think I was competitive towards high school, but I was competitive because I was with a group of friends who were all exceptional. And it's probably driven by curiosity and just wanting to be because we found it fun. We found it fun to do math. We found it fun to do physics. That's sort of what led me like a peer group. And peer group. I think I give a lot of I attribute a lot to the people I was around.
turns.zh: 我不认为人们会形容我有野心。人们也许在初中、高中早期会形容我无忧无虑。我认为我在高中时很有竞争力，但我有竞争力是因为我和一群都很出色的朋友在一起。这可能是由好奇心驱动的，只是想成为因为我觉得有趣。我们发现做数学很有趣。我们发现做物理很有趣。这就是引导我的同伴群体。同伴群体。我认为我把很多归因于我周围的人。

turns.en: Were you were you looking up to something in those growing up years? Was was there Narayan Murthy or somebody like that or in the US somebody that you looked up to?
turns.zh: 在你成长的岁月里，你有没有仰望过什么？有没有纳拉亚纳·穆尔蒂或类似的人，或者在美国有没有你仰望的人？

turns.en: No, no, there wasn't like a I I've one even back then and even till they've did like I am not the kind of person that like looks up at like role models or idols. Like that's just not my way of visualizing myself or the future. I think it was like much more day to day, which is like, oh, we want to go do this or this problem sounds hard or I'm with the bunch of friends where we're we're talking to each other about problems we're solving. You end up in this getting into IIT has this entrance exam that like is talked about which requires real amounts of hard work. Turns out, but if you're if you are someone who actually enjoys that kind of problem solving and learning and is surrounded by many such people who also happen to be really good. It just is the cheat code to be able to do it with perhaps less pain than other people.
turns.zh: 不，不，没有像……我甚至那时和直到现在都没有，我不是那种仰望榜样或偶像的人。那不是我想象自己或未来的方式。我认为它更像是日常的，比如，哦，我们想去做这个，或者这个问题听起来很难，或者我和一群朋友在一起，我们互相谈论我们正在解决的问题。你最终进入 IIT，有这个入学考试，人们谈论它，需要真正的努力。事实证明，但如果你是一个真正享受那种解决问题和学习的人，并且周围有很多这样的人，他们碰巧也很优秀。这就像是作弊码，能够以可能比其他人更少的痛苦做到这一点。

turns.en: And then when you landed in America in 2005 you went to Stanford for your PhD straight away and your plan was to be in academia, right?
turns.zh: 然后当你 2005 年抵达美国时，你直接去斯坦福攻读博士学位，你的计划是进入学术界，对吧？

turns.en: Plan is probably an overstated word. I think the the the journey I was on like after physics Olympiad went to IIT started doing computer science hadn't really done computers before then, right? Like so I went from math and physics to computers mostly because the smartest kids went to do computer science at the best institutions. So I was lucky enough to get in got to be there. As a computer scientist I was like more of a math person. So I did a fair amount of research during undergrad. So I really enjoyed solving hard research problems and I came to Stanford in part because one I wanted to just like it seemed like PhD was the path for me at the time to me because like my world wasn't broad enough to fully contemplate every other path. But I also knew that I didn't want to do the same kind of research I had done during undergrad. So I chose Stanford because it would be a fresh clean start relative to other institutions I could have gone to where I would continue the same research which I was already doing. At Stanford it's like okay we don't care who you are. Show up and figure you have the first year to figure out what research you're going to do and I change fields. My journey is to get more and more applied every step of the way perhaps a little bit impatient every step of the way. Like during undergrad I was fine doing like just writing proofs, right? I wanted to start building things and that started for me during my PhD.
turns.zh: 计划可能是一个夸大的词。我认为我走过的旅程，比如在物理奥林匹克之后去了 IIT，开始做计算机科学，之前并没有真正做过计算机，对吧？所以我从数学和物理转向计算机，主要是因为最聪明的孩子去最好的机构做计算机科学。所以我很幸运能进入那里。作为一个计算机科学家，我更像一个数学人。所以我在本科期间做了相当多的研究。所以我真的很喜欢解决困难的研究问题，我来斯坦福部分是因为一，我只是想，当时对我来说博士似乎是道路，因为我的世界不够广阔，无法完全考虑其他每条路。但我也知道我不想做我在本科期间做过的那种研究。所以我选择斯坦福，因为相对于其他我可以去的机构，它将是一个全新的开始，在那里我会继续我已经在做同样的研究。在斯坦福，就像好吧，我们不在乎你是谁。出现并弄清楚，你有第一年时间弄清楚你要做什么研究，我改变了领域。我的旅程是每一步都越来越应用，也许每一步都有点不耐烦。比如在本科期间，我可以只写证明，对吧？我想开始构建东西，这在我博士期间开始了。

turns.en: And then what made the switch to Twitter happen because that feels like a departure from solving math problems to becoming a junior engineer at Twitter?
turns.zh: 然后是什么让你转向 Twitter，因为那感觉像是从解决数学问题转向成为 Twitter 的初级工程师？

turns.en: Yeah, so I think early on in my PhD, I realized that I didn't want to be an academic, but I still enjoyed research. So then my next mental model became to do research but within industry. At the time, there were all of these labs like Microsoft Research, Google Research, Yahoo Research, AT&T Bell Labs like on its final legs. And so I thought like, okay, maybe you can have it all, right? Maybe you can keep doing research but also have an impact and do real things. And so through the PhD, through a bulk of the PhD, I thought that is where I wanted to be. But towards the end, I got even more disillusioned with the the sort of straddling the boundary of academia where I think like I got disillusioned by the peer feedback loop of other academics judge your work. Your output is a published paper of of sorts. Usually it is judged by others who are also not entirely living in the real world, right? And so it felt like a slow feedback loop. It felt like a low signal feedback loop. And I was getting impatient to like do things which were which felt more real and tangible. And so after doing like a lot of summer jobs at every industrial research lab, I gradually came to the realization like I should just like go build stuff. And then so it was a pretty last minute thing.
turns.zh: 是的，所以在我博士早期，我意识到我不想成为学者，但我仍然喜欢研究。所以我的下一个心智模型变成了在工业界做研究。当时，有所有这些实验室，如微软研究院、谷歌研究院、雅虎研究院、AT&T 贝尔实验室，就像在最后阶段。所以我想，好吧，也许你可以拥有一切，对吧？也许你可以继续做研究，但也有影响力，做真实的事情。所以在博士期间，大部分博士期间，我认为那就是我想去的地方。但到最后，我对 straddling 学术界边界的做法更加幻灭，我觉得我对其他学者评判你工作的同行反馈循环感到幻灭。你的输出是发表的论文，通常由其他也不完全生活在现实世界中的人评判，对吧？所以感觉像是一个缓慢的反馈循环。感觉像是一个低信号的反馈循环。我越来越不耐烦去做那些感觉更真实和 tangible 的事情。所以在上过每个工业研究实验室的很多暑期工作后，我逐渐意识到我应该去构建东西。然后所以这是一个相当最后一刻的事情。

turns.en: I think even like six months before ending up at Twitter, I would have said that I'm more likely to do research in industry than a software engineering job. And I ended up at Twitter mostly because I was obsessed with the product, right? Like it felt early but I was like I was on it.
turns.zh: 我觉得甚至在加入 Twitter 前六个月，我都会说我更可能去工业界做研究，而不是做软件工程。我最终去了 Twitter，主要是因为我痴迷于这个产品，对吧？当时感觉还很早期，但我就是迷上了它。

turns.en: You were a Twitter user—were you a consumer or were you actively tweeting?
turns.zh: 你是 Twitter 用户——你是消费者还是积极发推？

turns.en: I was very active. I think working at Twitter made me tweet less over time, but yeah, I was a heavy-duty producer and consumer prior to starting to work there.
turns.zh: 我非常活跃。我觉得在 Twitter 工作后，我发推反而少了，但没错，在开始工作之前，我是重度生产者和消费者。

turns.en: And that was a phenomenal run, right? You went from a junior engineer to their first distinguished engineer to the CTO to CEO, if I'm correct. And Twitter also went through a few eras at that time. It started when you joined—it was still a hit company but still small—then it became the public town square of the world. How were those early days at Twitter and how did it evolve in the various CEO journeys before you ended up taking over?
turns.zh: 那是一段非凡的历程，对吧？你从初级工程师到他们的首位杰出工程师，再到 CTO，再到 CEO，如果我没记错的话。而且 Twitter 当时也经历了几 个时代。你加入时它起步时还是一家热门公司但规模仍小，后来它成了世界的公共广场。Twitter 的早期日子是怎样的？在你接手之前，它经历了哪些 CEO 阶段？

turns.en: Yeah, so I started as a junior software engineer. I went there to work for the new ads team. So Twitter was already at the time a product that was starting to work. The biggest problem on the product was making it reliable, bringing in enough machines so that it would scale and you wouldn't see the fail whale. But on the other side, as the product was scaling, they needed to ultimately be a monetization story and Twitter started bringing in a small team to go build that. So that team essentially worked a little bit separate from the rest of the company to an extent. And I was a part of this early smallish team which we were really fortunate—the people who hired me there, they're not parallel. So some people from that team from that day are now at Parallel. I think it felt like a small elite team on a zero-to-one journey. And so it's not just working at Twitter, it's working on a problem which was fast moving. That team grew like you would think a rapidly scaling startup grows, right? From 10-odd people to hundreds of people in like a year and a half, from running a system on like four computers to 4,000 computers in a year and a half, to take revenue from almost nothing to like a couple billion in like two or three years. So that journey was particularly rewarding in that early couple of years because you get to figure out—I didn't know how to hire people, right? But I did so many interviews.
turns.zh: 是的，我一开始是初级软件工程师。我去那里是为了新的广告团队工作。当时 Twitter 已经是一个开始起势的产品。产品最大的问题是让它可靠，引入足够的机器以便扩展，这样你就不会看到失败鲸。但另一方面，随着产品扩展，他们最终需要有一个货币化的故事，Twitter 开始引入一个小团队来构建这个。所以那个团队在某种程度上与公司其他部分有点分开运作。我是这个早期小团队的一员，我们非常幸运——当时招聘我的人，他们不在 Parallel。所以当时那个团队的一些人现在在 Parallel。感觉就像一个小型精英团队在走从零到一的旅程。所以这不仅仅是在 Twitter 工作，而是在解决一个快速变化的问题。那个团队的增长就像你想象中快速扩张的初创公司一样，对吧？从大约 10 个人到一年半内数百人，从在四台电脑上运行系统到一年半内 4000 台电脑，从几乎零收入到两三年内几十亿美元。所以那早期几年的旅程特别有回报，因为你能摸索出——我不知道怎么招聘，对吧？但我做了很多面试。

turns.en: Yeah, so actually one of the questions I had for you was who taught you to go from an IC to a leader—hiring, culture—like we'll go into a lot of your operating principles later, but how were those years of learning? Were you bumping into a lot of mistakes and then just learning by yourself? Was there an influence on you?
turns.zh: 是的，其实我有个问题想问你：是谁教你从个人贡献者转变为领导者——招聘、文化——我们稍后会深入讨论你的很多运营原则，但那些年的学习是怎样的？你是不断犯错然后自己学习吗？有没有人对你产生影响？

turns.en: Of course, right? I think everyone around you influences you, every problem that you have to solve influences you. I remember it was early enough at Twitter that Twitter was not too organized. So for example, one of the things I distinctly remember was we needed to hire great people. One fine day—and I think it was 2011 or 2012, towards the end of the year. I was relatively new. I was like the most junior person around and I had this weird idea that we should go hire undergrads graduating college in IITs. And there's just no precedent for it at Twitter. Twitter had a university recruiting team that went to four universities in the US or something at the time, right? And so I was like I want to go do that, right? And we didn't have a track record of doing video interviews at the time, which today feels weird, but at the time was just true, right? We didn't have too many ways of doing immigrations for people. Or we didn't have too much precedent of that. But I literally showed up there and in like six hours of interviews with a bunch of people hired a bunch, many of whom became really influential engineers over time. But it was pure people showing initiative and people just going with it to letting you do things that you thought solve the problem of the day, which was hiring amazing people ASAP who were extremely talented. And so in the process though for hiring those—I don't know we hired maybe five or six people which was like hiring five people in a day for a small team was a big deal and five amazing people in a day. But we learned how to do video interviews. I was like the recruiting coordinator. I had printed offer letters for everyone because we didn't know who we would hire and there are some rules that you have to give the offers that same day. But you could do things, right? You could just go look at a problem and be like I think this is what I want to do and you be like let's go. And so that environment is the one that I think you learned in. I think people think that you learn by only making mistakes. I don't think that's true. People think that you learn by only imitating others. I think that is not true. Of course you have to learn from those things, right? You can't repeat every mistake, but you also can't entirely imitate others. But I think if you're given—there's a lot of like if you decide to solve something a certain way, it is often more possible than you believe if you just keep following through on it. Right? If you decide like to do things you can make them work.
turns.zh: 当然，对吧？我觉得你周围的每个人都会影响你，你必须解决的每个问题都会影响你。我记得当时 Twitter 还足够早期，组织性不太强。比如，我清楚记得的一件事是我们需要招聘优秀的人。有一天——我想是 2011 或 2012 年底。我相对较新。我是周围最初级的人，我有个奇怪的想法：我们应该去印度理工学院招聘即将毕业的本科生。这在 Twitter 没有先例。当时 Twitter 有一个大学招聘团队，去美国的四所大学之类的，对吧？所以我就说我想去做这个，对吧？当时我们没有视频面试的记录，今天听起来很奇怪，但当时就是事实，对吧？我们没有太多办法为人们办理移民。或者我们没有太多先例。但我真的去了那里，在大约六个小时的面试中，和一群人一起招聘了一批人，其中许多人后来成为非常有影响力的工程师。但这纯粹是人们展现主动性，人们顺其自然，让你做你认为能解决当天问题的事情，那就是尽快招聘极其优秀的杰出人才。所以在这个过程中，招聘那些人——我不知道，我们大概招了五六个人，对于一个小团队来说，一天招五个人是件大事，一天招五个优秀的人。但我们学会了如何进行视频面试。我就像招聘协调员。我为每个人打印了录用通知书，因为我们不知道会招谁，而且有些规则要求你当天发出录用通知。但你可以做事，对吧？你可以直接去看一个问题，然后说我觉得这就是我想做的，然后你说让我们去吧。所以那种环境就是你学习的环境。我认为人们认为你只有通过犯错才能学习。我不认为那是真的。人们认为你只有通过模仿他人才能学习。我认为那不是真的。当然你必须从这些事情中学习，对吧？你不能重复每一个错误，但你也无法完全模仿他人。但我认为如果你被给予——很多时候，如果你决定以某种方式解决某事，只要你坚持到底，它往往比你相信的更可能实现。对吧？如果你决定做事情，你就能让它们成功。

turns.en: Yeah. But clearly you know that environment was there for everyone to do things. So clearly you still rose through the ranks. When we were talking earlier, you'd mentioned like you were just used to this idea of attacking the problems that you think are hard. What's the reason you were able to rise to their first distinguished engineer, the CTO, the CEO?
turns.zh: 是的。但显然你知道那个环境对每个人都是开放的。所以显然你还是晋升了。我们之前聊天时，你提到你习惯于攻击你认为困难的问题。你能够晋升为他们的首位杰出工程师、CTO、CEO 的原因是什么？

turns.en: No, I think so one prerequisite as I've been saying right like in many environments, no matter what you do that is not a possibility, right? And so I think in some sense Twitter of that era was special in that it was a possibility. Number two I think I got lucky to an extent. Like you need luck for journeys like this always. The thing I if I look back at like what I did right and like the common element there I think it was two things. One I think I always like to be with and around really capable people who push me to do more and push collectively you raise your ambition as well as capability simultaneously. Like who are those people with whom that happens? And I don't think I would have described it that way back then, but to me it's like a feeling that you look for in surrounding yourself with people and problems of that nature. The second thing I think I was both good at and got lucky with is I think I would look at Twitter and what we were doing a little bit from the outside in.
turns.zh: 不，我认为正如我一直在说的，一个前提是，在许多环境中，无论你做什么，那都不是一种可能性，对吧？所以我认为在某种意义上，那个时代的 Twitter 很特别，因为它是一种可能性。第二，我认为我在某种程度上很幸运。像这样的旅程总是需要运气。如果我回顾我做对的事情以及其中的共同元素，我认为有两点。第一，我总是喜欢和真正有能力的人在一起，他们推动我做更多，并集体推动你同时提升野心和能力。比如那些与你一起发生这种事的人是谁？我当时不会那样描述，但对我来说，这是一种你在周围寻找的人和问题的那种感觉。第二，我认为我既擅长又幸运的是，我会稍微从外向内看 Twitter 和我们正在做的事情。

turns.en: I think today I describe it again. I wouldn't have described it this way back then. But like I wanted to work on—you know how every employee at every company sits around thinking, if I was the CEO we would be doing X, right? And I had that vibe about me saying, so what do I think? I would try to figure out how to collect the band—like how to drive influence, collect the engineers, the PMs, to be in the place where you could as a tiny group do things that you believed should be happening and would be happening if you were the CEO but weren't fully happening or weren't getting the attention they deserved.
turns.zh: 我想今天我会这样描述它。当时我不会这么说。但就像我想做的——你知道每个公司的每个员工都会坐在那里想，如果我是 CEO，我们会做 X，对吧？我身上就有那种气质，说，那我是怎么想的？我会试着弄清楚如何聚集一群人——如何施加影响力，聚集工程师、产品经理，让你作为一个小团队能够做那些你认为应该发生、而且如果你当 CEO 就会发生、但当时并未完全发生或没有得到应有重视的事情。

turns.en: When you were not yet CEO, what's an example of an initiative you were like, guys come on we need to be doing this, and then you just did it?
turns.zh: 当你还不是 CEO 的时候，有没有一个例子，你当时说“伙计们，我们得做这个”，然后你就去做了？

turns.en: I think these were simple things. These are not like some crazy big deep insights, right? Like I used to work on ads. Ads was this separate siloed team—slightly siloed, not fully siloed—and you build ads, you collect a bunch of—you build a bunch of interesting machine learning systems because what is ads? It's like matchmaking with machine learning. Twitter at the time used to do a reverse chronological timeline and there was almost a religion at the company to not use too much machine learning when it came to the core product, right? So I'm there sitting around building ads. I was like a data geek, right? So I'm looking at Twitter going public, we built ads, now you can see if you do the math on the growth engine of the company—it to me appeared that it could stall out at under a hundred million DAU, the growth engine of the business. So we spent years dealing with, oh Twitter's growing so fast we can't roll servers in or keep the site up, and all of a sudden we were going to end up in a world where, oh god, the product is now flatlining in its growth potential, right? And it didn't get there, but you could forecast that in a year that's where we would be if you looked at the data carefully enough, right? So I'm like, okay, no one seems to be paying attention to this, this religion against machine learning. I'm going to abandon ads, I'm going to figure out how to show up on the product side and work with a collection of people where we would go transform the product to drive long-term durable growth. It's like very simple. It wasn't like the top-down strategic direction for the company yet, but a year later that's what it sort of became, right? So it's like these kind of obvious-ish ideas, but the right people focused execution with a small group to prove and change the rest of the company around it, right? So I did that among with other people and showed a lot of initiative there, fought as you can imagine some internal battles because these cultural things are ingrained. And I think there were a few more of these kinds of things.
turns.zh: 我觉得这些都是简单的事情。不是什么疯狂宏大的深刻洞见，对吧？比如我以前做广告。广告是一个独立的团队——稍微独立，不是完全独立——你构建广告，你聚集一堆——你构建一堆有趣的机器学习系统，因为广告是什么？就像是机器学习的匹配。当时 Twitter 用的是按时间倒序的时间线，公司里几乎有一种宗教般的信条，就是核心产品不要用太多机器学习，对吧？所以我在那里做广告。我是个数据极客，对吧？所以我看着 Twitter 上市，我们构建了广告，现在你可以看到，如果你对公司的增长引擎做一下数学计算——在我看来，它可能会在不到一亿日活用户时停滞，业务的增长引擎。所以我们花了几年时间应对，哦，Twitter 增长太快了，我们无法部署服务器或保持网站运行，然后突然之间我们就要进入一个世界，天哪，产品现在增长潜力趋于平缓了，对吧？它没有到那一步，但如果你足够仔细地看数据，你可以预测一年后我们就会到那里，对吧？所以我想，好吧，似乎没人在关注这个，这种反对机器学习的宗教。我要放弃广告，我要想办法出现在产品侧，和一群人合作，去改造产品以推动长期持久的增长。这很简单。这还不是公司自上而下的战略方向，但一年后它差不多变成了那样，对吧？所以就是这些看似明显的想法，但合适的人专注执行，用一个小团队去证明并改变公司其他部分，对吧？所以我和其他人一起做了这件事，展现了很大的主动性，如你所料，打了一些内部战，因为这些文化的东西根深蒂固。我想还有几个类似的事情。

turns.en: What did you change in the first three to six months once you became the CEO then?
turns.zh: 那么你成为 CEO 后的头三到六个月里改变了什么？

turns.en: Plenty. Some popular, some not popular. Biggest picture, right? When you—I had worked at the company for almost, I would say 10 years by then, right? Or more than 10 years, 10 years. I always saw my job as looking at the people around me, the problems around me, and figuring out how I could maximally contribute, right? So there were periods where I would be a solo IC. That was my preference even while in leadership. There were periods where I would manage reasonable size organizations trying to figure out how to hire somebody better to do that so I could go do something else. And so but I mostly wanted to be flexible in adapting myself to the best of my ability to maximally contribute to the company or the team. The face shift you have to go through when you become the CEO is—at least for me, the advice I give and what I internalized for myself—was that you no longer adapt, try to adapt yourself. You challenge yourself. But you adapt the company to who you are. Because if you are trying to fit into somebody else's shoes, you're not going to create the best version of the company and that is a bad thing to do. You're doing injustice to the potential of the company.
turns.zh: 很多。有些受欢迎，有些不受欢迎。从大处看，对吧？当时我已经在公司工作了将近——我想说到那时已经 10 年了，对吧？或者超过 10 年，10 年。我一直把我的工作看作观察周围的人、周围的问题，并弄清楚我如何能做出最大贡献，对吧？所以有段时间我是个独立的个人贡献者。即使在领导层中，那也是我的偏好。有段时间我管理合理规模的团队，试图弄清楚如何雇佣更好的人来做那件事，这样我可以去做别的事。所以我主要想灵活地调整自己，尽我所能为公司或团队做出最大贡献。成为 CEO 后你必须经历的面貌转变是——至少对我来说，我给出的建议和我内化的——是你不再适应，试图适应自己。你挑战自己。但你让公司适应你是谁。因为如果你试图穿别人的鞋，你不会创造出公司的最佳版本，那是一件坏事。你对公司的潜力不公平。

turns.en: Say that actually—this is a great point you've made. Is that a personality thing? Like what—what are you trying to shape the company towards your personality, towards your vision, what all of it?
turns.zh: 说真的——你提出了一个很好的观点。那是性格问题吗？比如你试图把公司塑造成你的个性、你的愿景，还是所有这一切？

turns.en: All of it, right? I think it's like your personality, your vision, how you like—how your mental model of the company. Are you a product first person? Are you an edge first person? Are you a data person? Are you being counter? The three types of CEOs should organize their teams differently. They should hire differently. They should have different kinds of executive team, executive team meetings. Who they hire is a function of them. It should be a compliment to you. Previously I was trying to shape shift myself to be most incrementally valuable around the CEO or the rest of the leadership team or the needs of the business, right? Now all of a sudden if you take a five year view, you have to transform the business. The Twitter job was—Twitter was not a done deal. Like there was like a real business to build and scale. And the only way that would happen is for me to transform it into what I thought it would be, right? So you have to own the thing and own yourself.
turns.zh: 所有这一切，对吧？我认为这就像你的个性、你的愿景、你喜欢的——你对公司的心理模型。你是产品优先的人吗？你是工程优先的人吗？你是数据型的人吗？你是反其道而行的人吗？这三种类型的 CEO 应该以不同的方式组织他们的团队。他们应该以不同的方式招聘。他们应该有不同类型的高管团队、高管团队会议。他们雇佣谁是他们的函数。它应该是对你的补充。以前我试图改变自己，以在 CEO 或其他领导团队或业务需求周围成为最有增量价值的人，对吧？现在突然之间，如果你以五年为视角，你必须改造业务。Twitter 的工作是——Twitter 并不是一个已成定局的事情。就像有一个真正的业务要建立和扩展。而唯一的方式就是让我把它改造成我认为它应该成为的样子，对吧？所以你必须拥有这个东西，并拥有你自己。

turns.en: What was the thing you thought it needed to be? Like yeah, what was that?
turns.zh: 你认为它需要成为什么？比如，那是什么？

turns.en: I think Twitter was already—and I think it's proven today that the product had durability. The product needed to scale to more people. And importantly the business needed to get stronger, right? So, I think I thought Twitter was too large. So, we were actually working on making it a better business over time partly through being a leaner, more agile team. But partly I think there was so much more machine learning—as I would have said it during that time—to be done on both the product, on all the issues around content moderation, on ads. I don't think Twitter was like as machine learning built even for that day as it could even should have been. And so I think that was part of the hypothesis in building.
turns.zh: 我认为 Twitter 已经——而且我认为今天已经证明产品具有持久性。产品需要扩展到更多人。更重要的是，业务需要变得更强，对吧？所以，我认为我认为 Twitter 太大了。所以，我们实际上在努力随着时间的推移使它成为更好的业务，部分是通过成为一个更精简、更敏捷的团队。但部分我认为还有更多的机器学习——正如我当时会说的——要在产品、内容审核的所有问题、广告上做。我不认为 Twitter 即使在那时也像它可能甚至应该的那样是机器学习构建的。所以我认为那是构建假设的一部分。

turns.en: Were there cultural changes also that you felt strongly about or did Twitter have a through line in its culture from the days you joined to what it became?
turns.zh: 是否也有你强烈感受到的文化变革，或者 Twitter 的文化从你加入的日子到它变成的样子有一条贯穿线？

turns.en: No, culture evolved quite a lot over the years I was there. I think yeah, I think I for example like you asked me earlier what were the things you did in the first three to six months, right? To shape the company around me, I made a pretty significant sort of changes to the leadership team around me. A lot of it was attributable to me being a different person, needing a different structure, right? Some of it was attributable to me wanting to transform culture. For example, one of the things I did—I think I took the job end of November or something.
turns.zh: 不，文化在我在那里的这些年里演变了很多。我想是的，我想比如你之前问我头三到六个月你做了什么，对吧？为了塑造我周围的公司，我对周围的领导团队做了相当大的改变。很多是因为我是一个不同的人，需要不同的结构，对吧？有些是因为我想改变文化。例如，我做的一件事——我想我是在 11 月底左右接任的。

turns.en: In December, I asked the team to do, after several years of Twitter not doing it, some amount of employee performance conversations, management ratings, whatever you might describe it, right? Now these things feel extremely corporate, right? But I think they are a signal on what you value. And it was important to me in part because I wanted to—Twitter had been a place which hadn't for the last several years done serious performance management, which goes towards both letting go of people not performing and empowering and rewarding the top performers. I think there are these two different dimensions. I grew up in an era early on at Twitter where I saw both of these things happen. I was at Twitter when we did a round of layoffs, in fact two rounds of layoffs, right? I experienced what it felt like going in. I experienced what the company could do after, and those things sort of shaped my view. So I was wanting to drive a culture towards performance, and I think all of these performance and ratings, processes and systems at scale are extraordinarily flawed. But the one thing they do is they send a signal. Now all the data that comes out of it is noisy and you have to exercise great amounts of judgment as you use it. But it's really important to change things. And so month one I decide to do something which is not popular at the time, right? Like not among people, not among managers, not among leadership, right? But it was popular among some subset of them. And I wanted to empower that subset.
turns.zh: 去年 12 月，我让团队做了一些员工绩效对话、管理层评级之类的事情，而 Twitter 已经好几年没做过了。这些事情听起来非常公司化，但我觉得它们传递了你重视什么的信号。这对我很重要，部分是因为我希望——Twitter 过去几年一直没有做严肃的绩效管理，而绩效管理既包括让表现不佳的人离开，也包括赋能和奖励顶尖表现者。我认为这是两个不同的维度。我在 Twitter 早期经历过这两件事。我经历过裁员，实际上两轮裁员。我体验过裁员进行时的感受，也体验过公司之后能做什么，这些塑造了我的看法。所以我想推动一种注重绩效的文化，而我认为所有大规模的绩效和评级流程与系统都极其有缺陷。但它们至少能发出一个信号。当然，从中得出的所有数据都有噪音，使用时需要大量判断。但改变现状真的很重要。所以第一个月我决定做一件当时不受欢迎的事，在员工、管理者、领导层中都不受欢迎，但在其中一部分人中受欢迎。我想赋能那部分人。

turns.en: And then towards the end of that stint, maybe the last six to 12 months, you also had a pretty—I mean, in some ways few operators have felt that kind of pressure, right? Running the public town square of the world, Elon's takeover bid, the ups and downs of it. I'm less interested in the news story there, the sensationalism, more like the operators. Like how was it to lead through that phase of six to 12 months when the takeover is happening, not happening, Elon is tweeting all about it? How did you manage to lead the team and what was going through your own mind as a CEO then?
turns.zh: 然后在那段任期的尾声，也许是最后 6 到 12 个月，你也经历了一段相当——我的意思是，很少有运营者感受过那种压力，对吧？运营着全球公共城市广场，埃隆的收购要约，起起伏伏。我对那里的新闻故事和耸人听闻不太感兴趣，更关注运营者本身。在收购发生又不发生、埃隆不停发推的那 6 到 12 个月里，带领团队是怎样的体验？作为当时的 CEO，你如何管理团队，自己心里又在想什么？

turns.en: So I think the real interesting operating period was perhaps prior to signing the merger agreement, right? Through that period we were operating on what my plan would be, which was in fact planning a—I think this is public data, it's out there on the proxy statements—that we were planning a significant reduction in force, layoff at the company. In parallel there was a public conversation brewing around potential takeovers in the media, which was a little bit off reality. And then a private conversation brewing with the other side around whether that was likely and whether that was real, right? And so that few weeks of navigating these multiple things and simultaneously operating in an intense period—like the other thing that was happening then was the war in Ukraine had just started, right? Which was causing the entire business to evolve. So you're navigating that reality, the business implications, the layoff plans and a potential two-sided M&A conversation all at the same time. In a way, some of these were my proactive plans. But then there was this confluence of multiple things coming at us all at the same time. So that one month was perhaps the most interesting or intense. You do learn a lot—like I learned about public company M&A and all of the things around it in a way that I wouldn't have known. But I think once the merger agreement was signed, it was perhaps not interesting. It takes a period to close. We found ourselves in a little bit of no man's land. It's no man's land because you can't paint the long-term vision, especially in a case where there isn't deep cooperation on the two sides, which fell apart within a week, right? So now the best way to run a company is to have a long-term plan and ambition and a vision and a collection of steps that get you there, that put you on the path to learning. Like that's the only thing I know, right? And once you take away your capability to credibly describe a long-term ambition, vision, future for the company, that's a hard operating environment, right? And you had lawyers on almost every decision knowing that this was looking like a contested moment. Now, credit to the leadership team there, Twitter continued operating well. We managed despite the uncertainty, every advertiser feeling the uncertainty and wondering if they should pull out. Our teams managed to not let that happen through this period of uncertainty. We shipped a lot of valuable things in that period that I'm proud of. We managed to do a lot of performance management in letting people who were not performing go through that period too, rigorous through rigorous management. So because the framework is like the deal isn't closed until it's closed. So you are now operating in this weird dual reality of—listen, we are committed to closing this deal and will put in every effort in the court of law to make sure it closes. And simultaneously we are operating like it won't. Because one day we might be on our own and we have to have momentum, we have to have great people, we have to be shipping things, we have to have product velocity. And so you're now—and I could keep these two contradictory things in my mind. It is very hard to have thousands of people operate in this sort of weird dual reality.
turns.zh: 我认为真正有趣的运营期也许是在签署合并协议之前。那段时间我们按照我的计划运作，实际上是在计划一次大规模的裁员——我想这是公开数据，在委托书里都有——我们计划在公司进行大规模裁员。与此同时，媒体上围绕潜在收购的公开讨论正在酝酿，与实际情况有些出入。然后与另一方私下里也在酝酿对话，讨论收购是否可能、是否真实。所以那几周要应对这些多重事情，同时还要在紧张时期运营——当时还发生了另一件事，乌克兰战争刚刚开始，导致整个业务都在演变。所以你要同时应对那个现实、业务影响、裁员计划以及潜在的双边并购对话。某种程度上，其中一些是我主动的计划。但后来多种事情同时涌来。所以那一个月也许是最有趣或最紧张的。你确实学到很多——比如我学到了上市公司并购及其相关的一切，否则我不会知道。但我认为一旦合并协议签署，也许就没那么有趣了。完成交易需要一段时间。我们发现自己处于某种无人区。之所以是无人区，是因为你无法描绘长期愿景，尤其是在双方没有深度合作的情况下，而合作在一周内就破裂了。所以现在运营公司的最佳方式是有一个长期计划和雄心、愿景以及一系列步骤，让你走上学习之路。我只知道这个。一旦你失去了可信地描述公司长期雄心、愿景和未来的能力，那就是一个艰难的运营环境。而且几乎每个决策都有律师参与，因为知道这看起来像是一个有争议的时刻。现在，要归功于那里的领导团队，Twitter 继续运营良好。尽管有不确定性，每个广告商都感受到不确定性并想知道是否应该撤出，我们的团队设法不让这种情况发生。那段时间我们发布了许多有价值的东西，我为此感到自豪。我们也做了大量绩效管理，让表现不佳的人离开，通过严格的管理。因为框架是交易在完成之前都不算完成。所以你现在在一个奇怪的双重现实中运营：一方面，我们致力于完成这笔交易，并将尽一切努力在法庭上确保完成。同时，我们又在像交易不会完成一样运营。因为有一天我们可能会独立，我们必须有势头，必须有优秀的人，必须发布产品，必须有产品速度。所以你现在——我可以在头脑中保持这两个矛盾的事情。但让数千人在这种奇怪的双重现实中运营是非常困难的。

turns.en: So how were you communicating that? Because I agree that dual reality seems like extremely tough and it's kind of also maybe not a replicable thing. I don't know if there are any lessons that you can take to parallel from that.
turns.zh: 那你是如何沟通的？因为我同意这种双重现实看起来极其艰难，而且可能也不是可复制的事情。我不知道你能否从中总结出一些可借鉴的教训。

turns.en: No, I think there are base level lessons you can take, right? I think I generally was, to the extent possible, I was honest and direct with people. You can actually go see what I was doing because every time I did a lot of all hands through this period where the entire company got to ask me questions. I did several of them and they all leaked, right? Like there was media in every one of them. And so yeah, that's out there, right? It's just a weird environment. I think the lessons you take away from that are sometimes you don't have agency on certain things. Like fiduciary responsibility takes over and like—I was not born to be only a fiduciary, right? But I think at some point that's what that job became. When I took the job, I didn't think it was likely that that's what the job would become, right? And if you told me that's what I was signing up for was like a primarily fiduciary for a period—
turns.zh: 不，我认为有一些基础层面的教训可以吸取。我总体上尽可能对人诚实直接。你实际上可以看到我在做什么，因为这段时间我做了很多全员大会，整个公司都可以问我问题。我做了几次，全都泄露了，每次都有媒体在场。所以，那些都在外面了。这只是一个奇怪的环境。我认为从中得到的教训是，有时候你对某些事情没有自主权。比如信托责任接管了——我不是生来就只做信托责任人，但某个时候那份工作就变成了那样。当我接受这份工作时，我不认为它很可能会变成那样。如果你告诉我，我签约的就是在一段时间内主要做信托责任人——

transcript.sec: Reflections on Twitter and doing right by people

turns.en: Like, that's not the most exciting thing when you're trying to build for a positive-sum game, to end up in this sort of zero-sum contested M&A transaction, even if that's the best return in the board's view for the shareholders. So I think it was not necessarily something you can take a lot of lessons from in terms of doing right by people. Like all the people that I worked with, whether or not we made hard decisions with them, I feel pretty good that today if you go talk to them — people who are at least close to me, and even a few steps removed from me — they think I conducted myself in a way that I'm proud of.
turns.zh: 当你想要构建一个正和博弈时，最终却陷入这种零和、充满争议的并购交易，这可不是最令人兴奋的事，即便在董事会看来这是对股东最好的回报。所以我觉得，在“善待他人”这件事上，未必能从中总结出很多经验。和我共事过的所有人，无论我们是否对他们做过艰难的决定，我今天都挺欣慰——如果你现在去问他们，至少和我关系近的人，甚至隔了几层关系的人，都认为我的行事方式让我感到自豪。

turns.en: So you told me earlier you had never planned to be a founder, right, till that moment. So what post-Twitter — what went through your mind? I think you went quiet for a couple of years almost. What went through your mind? Why be a founder at the age of 40?
turns.zh: 你之前跟我说过，你从没打算成为创始人，对吧，直到那一刻。那么离开 Twitter 之后——你当时在想什么？我记得你差不多沉寂了两年。你当时脑子里在想什么？为什么要在 40 岁去当创始人？

turns.en: 40 is young. Why be a founder? I don't know. So, a couple of things. When I took the CEO job at Twitter, it was like a real process, right? You have a bunch of interviews with the board. You have to think about what you're going to build, what your vision is, what your ambition is. It's like a real intense six to eight weeks prior to announcing, of intense work. And that work — at least my process was — I put a lot of fuel into myself and a lot of energy. You load yourself up with energy to go for it, and before you get to refuel again, it's going to be like five to seven years, and you're going to go all in and do everything you have, because that's what it will take to transform this already large, consequential thing into something it could be or should be, right? So now you have all of a sudden all of this unspent fuel sitting around without a clear output channel for it. Like, which way do I point this thing? I put all of it in over this intense period. Now I have all of this reserve. Like, what do I do with it? And I was pretty open-minded initially, but I was hacking and building, and it's like I've said before, it's a good time to be a technical person who was unemployed. It was as good a year as you want — you could choose to be in that position, right? And in that position, it felt like the world was about to change and transform. And whenever I looked at working in places, it felt to me that, one, I wanted to work with a small number of people. Like this whole desire of a special small number of people that I get to choose — that was almost the most important criterion — to something technically hard where I wanted to be much more technical again. Like, I think you lose a little bit of touch, even if you try really hard, with the technical work. If you are in a large place as a senior executive, you can allocate only so much of your time to it. And I really wanted — I was starting to write a bunch of code again and I was really enjoying being in the weeds on just technically solving problems with my own hands, in a real way. And so all the big jobs felt to me like they didn't pull me in. And so I relatively quickly realized — like maybe two, three months — that I would have to become a founder. But then it was not clear what I wanted to do.
turns.zh: 40 岁很年轻啊。为什么当创始人？我也不知道。有几件事吧。我接任 Twitter CEO 时，那是一个很正式的过程，对吧？你要和董事会进行一堆面试。你得思考你要构建什么、你的愿景是什么、你的抱负是什么。在正式宣布之前，有大概六到八周极其高强度的工作。而那段工作——至少我的做法是——我给自己加了很多燃料、很多能量。你把自己装满能量去冲刺，而下一次补充燃料之前，可能要过五到七年，你要全力以赴、倾尽所有，因为要把这个已经很大、很有影响力的事物改造成它可能或应该成为的样子，就需要这样。于是突然间，你有了所有这些没花出去的燃料，却没有明确的输出通道。我该把这东西指向哪里？我在那段高强度时期把所有能量都投进去了，现在我有这么多储备，我拿它怎么办？我一开始心态挺开放的，但我一直在写代码、做东西，就像我以前说过的，对一个失业的技术人来说，那是个好时机。你想处在那个位置的话，那一年再好不过了。在那个位置上，感觉世界即将改变、即将转型。而每当我考虑去某些地方工作时，我感觉：第一，我想和少数人一起工作。这种“由我挑选一小群特别的人”的渴望，几乎是最重要的标准；第二，要做技术上很难的事，我想重新变得更技术。我觉得即便你非常努力，在大机构里做高管，你对技术工作的手感也会有点脱节，你能分配在上面的时间就那么多。而我真的很想——我又开始写很多代码，我真的很享受深入细节、用自己的双手实实在在地解决技术问题。所以那些大公司的工作，感觉都吸引不了我。于是我相对快地意识到——大概两三个月吧——我可能必须去当创始人。但当时还不清楚我想做什么。

turns.en: Well, what can you — on this idea?
turns.zh: 那你能讲讲——这个想法是怎么来的？

turns.en: I think the idea found me. I wasn't proactively looking for this idea. I was proactively perhaps looking for other ideas, running in other dimensions. And this was like the side hustle, which was just like my hobby or fun — write fun code and then, you know, you're trying to understand various markets and dynamics and finding a point of view on various things. And you know, I'm the engineer who ended up being like, okay, I'm going to actually write an agent to make my life in doing so easier. And at the time agents didn't work. We were on pretty bad models. But I found myself spending more time doing that rather than actually doing the work I signed myself up to do, right? And then over time this thing became an obsession of sorts, and then you start thinking about, oh, these are all the problems I see. But really, what will happen if agents work? They don't work yet. What does it take to make them work? If they work, what happens? What happens to the web if they work? And it started to germinate that agents will eventually work. I had spent a lot of time with labs and researchers through this journey, and I was a believer that models will keep getting better. Agents will work. If they worked, I made up that they'd use the web a thousand X more. And if that happened, you'd have to invent new technology — really exciting — new business models — really exciting. And it felt like I had extraordinary confidence in that moment that this was just going to happen. And to me it felt, in that moment, obvious. When I spoke to others, it didn't yet feel obvious. So the same trick of, oh, Twitter needs machine learning in the consumer product, because how else do you use people's time most effectively when they choose to spend five minutes on Twitter and show them the most relevant, fun stuff? It felt obvious. It wasn't happening. This thing felt similarly obvious. Yet others around me didn't believe me, by and large.
turns.zh: 我觉得是想法找到了我。我并不是主动在找这个想法。我主动在找的也许是别的想法，在别的维度上探索。而这个东西像是副业，纯粹是爱好或好玩——写点有趣的代码，然后试着理解各种市场和动态，对各种事情形成自己的观点。你知道，我就是那个工程师，最后变成：好吧，我要真的写一个智能体，让我做这件事的生活更轻松。当时智能体根本不好用，我们用的模型还很差。但我发现自己花在这上面的时间，比花在我本该做的工作上还多，对吧？然后随着时间推移，这东西变成了一种痴迷，然后你开始想：哦，这些是我看到的所有问题。但真正的问题是，如果智能体能用了会怎样？它们现在还不行。要让它们能用需要什么？如果它们能用了，会发生什么？如果它们能用了，网络会变成什么样？然后一个念头开始萌芽：智能体终将能用。在这段旅程中，我和很多实验室、研究者待了很久，我坚信模型会持续变好，智能体会能用。如果它们能用了，我推测它们使用网络的频率会高出一千倍。如果那发生了，你就必须发明新技术——非常令人兴奋——新的商业模式——非常令人兴奋。那一刻我有一种非凡的信心，觉得这一定会发生。对我来说，那一刻它显而易见。但我和别人聊时，他们还不觉得显而易见。就像同样的套路：哦，Twitter 的消费产品需要机器学习，因为当人们选择在 Twitter 上花五分钟时，你还能怎么最有效地利用他们的时间，给他们看最相关、最有趣的内容？那感觉显而易见，但当时并没有发生。这件事感觉同样显而易见，可我周围大多数人并不相信我。

turns.en: So let's double-click on it. This is Parallel Web — it's search for agents, right? So why do agents need a different web search? What's different about how agents search than humans?
turns.zh: 那我们深入聊聊。这是 Parallel Web——是给智能体用的搜索，对吧？为什么智能体需要不一样的网络搜索？智能体搜索和人类搜索有什么不同？

turns.en: A lot, right? First, let's take the top-down perspective. If agents are going to use the web 1000X more, can you build 1000X the search infra that Google has built to support? I bet no. Okay. So now you have to have an argument that you can do something novel and unique. So you ask the question, what will this thing look like? And here's what you have. You're seeing the best capability show up at the hardware layer and GPUs. You want a lot of memory, you want lots of memory bandwidth, you want flops. Get GPUs. What if you decided to frame the web search problem as a problem to go solve it primarily using GPUs, over the generations of commodity GPUs? Second, these models are getting better. The other thing that's happening is, holding capability constant, you're going to be able to make the model smaller and smaller and smaller. And so now you will be able to distill into a much smaller model a lot of intelligence in a very broad-based way to build your anchor. So this is the dimension which is new — hardware and technology advancements as it relates to AI is going to allow us to build something which you couldn't have built a year ago or two years ago. That's number one. Number two, agents don't behave like humans on the web. So if you think about it, let's talk from a few dimensions. Inputs. A human going to a search engine, their input is a short, underspecified search query.
turns.zh: 差别很大，对吧？首先，从自上而下的视角看。如果智能体使用网络的频率要高出一千倍，你能建出 Google 所建搜索基础设施的一千倍来支撑吗？我赌不能。好，那你就得论证你能做出新颖独特的东西。于是你问：这东西会是什么样？而你手上有什么？你看到最强的能力出现在硬件层和 GPU 上。你想要大内存、大内存带宽、大算力。那就用 GPU。如果你决定把网络搜索问题框定为一个主要用 GPU 来解决的问题，依托一代代商品化 GPU 呢？第二，这些模型在变好。另一件正在发生的事是，在能力不变的前提下，你能把模型做得越来越小。于是你现在能把大量智能以非常广泛的方式蒸馏进一个小得多的模型，作为你的锚点。所以这个维度是新的——与 AI 相关的硬件和技术进步，将让我们能构建一年前或两年前造不出来的东西。这是第一点。第二点，智能体在网络上的行为不像人类。你想想，我们从几个维度来谈。输入。人类去搜索引擎，输入的是一个简短、信息不完整的搜索词。

turns.en: You're sometimes even using autocomplete, right? So mostly we don't tell the search engine what we want because we are impatient and we haven't even thought about it, right? Like you're trying to do something and you write two queries and then you go on this random walk of clicking on links, reading paragraphs, going back, searching more. That is how humans work. Agents are happy to write a session's worth as a query, right? For a human search engine, the output is 10 blue links so that you can go on your random walk, right? For an agent, the output is a collection of let's call them tokens to put in the context window that give the agent its next set of action space, correct? Which isn't just clicking on links, right? Number three, think of this human search engine. It monetizes at a certain rate. It has a certain latency profile to it. And those two things roughly tell you what kind of compute to throw at the problem and what kind of architecture to use, right? So it monetizes better than I think agentic traffic will because agentic traffic will be 1000X. Two, the latency profile on humans is humans are like a page loading between 500 milliseconds, it's great, right? It takes two seconds, it's really slow and annoyed. If it takes 400 milliseconds instead of 500 milliseconds, you won't even notice. Right? So there's a sweet spot you hit in page loads and search. With agents, there's high variance here, right? Like you think about a voice agent. If you take 500 milliseconds, 600 milliseconds for a voice agent, it feels too long a pause before the agent can talk back to you if you just do the math. Also, the entire premise of agents is humans essentially have a one second SLA in life, right? Like we want things to be interactive on the web, loading a page, talking voice agent coming back in subsecond. Agent's entire promise is you're going to be able to do more within each turn, right? So you ideally want search in an interactive setting to go from this sort of 500 millisecond thing to a 50, 100, 200 millisecond thing depending on the use case. But in the background agent context, search can take an hour. Who cares? It's working overnight, right? So now you have this extreme variance in what could be useful. And this open canvas to build entirely new technology around entirely new optimization points. The input is different, the output is different, your compute budget is different, your latency budget is different. What we've solved historically is this one narrow slice of it.
turns.zh: 你有时甚至会用自动补全，对吧？所以大多数时候我们不会告诉搜索引擎我们想要什么，因为我们没耐心，甚至还没想清楚，对吧？比如你在做某件事，你写了两个查询，然后就开始随机点击链接、阅读段落、返回、再搜索。这就是人类的工作方式。智能体则乐意把一次会话的量写成一个查询，对吧？对于人类搜索引擎，输出是 10 条蓝色链接，这样你可以继续随机漫步，对吧？对于智能体，输出是一组我们称之为 token 的东西，放入上下文窗口，给智能体下一组行动空间，对吧？这不仅仅是点击链接，对吧？第三，想想这个人类搜索引擎。它以一定的速率变现。它有一定的延迟特征。这两件事大致告诉你该投入什么样的算力，以及该用什么架构，对吧？所以它的变现能力比我认为的智能体流量要好，因为智能体流量将是 1000 倍。第二，人类的延迟特征是，人类就像页面加载在 500 毫秒之间，那很好，对吧？如果花两秒钟，那就真的很慢，很烦人。如果花 400 毫秒而不是 500 毫秒，你甚至不会注意到。对吧？所以在页面加载和搜索中有一个最佳点。对于智能体，这里方差很大，对吧？比如你想想语音智能体。如果你花 500 毫秒、600 毫秒，对于语音智能体来说，感觉停顿太长，智能体才能回话，如果你算一下的话。而且，智能体的整个前提是人类在生活中基本上有一秒的 SLA，对吧？比如我们希望网络上的东西是交互式的，加载页面、语音智能体在亚秒级内回复。智能体的全部承诺是你在每一轮中能做得更多，对吧？所以理想情况下，你希望交互式环境中的搜索从这种 500 毫秒的东西变成 50、100、200 毫秒的东西，取决于用例。但在后台智能体上下文中，搜索可以花一个小时。谁在乎？它整夜都在工作，对吧？所以现在你有这种极端的方差，什么可能有用。以及这个开放的画布，围绕全新的优化点构建全新的技术。输入不同，输出不同，你的算力预算不同，你的延迟预算不同。我们历史上解决的是这狭窄的一片。

turns.en: So it does feel to your point a lot of moving pieces, but what's the Can you actually talk about like what's the hardest part you've realized in the years of building now like which you may have even under appreciated when you were getting started on this journey? What's the hardest technical part?
turns.zh: 所以确实如你所说，有很多变动部分，但你能谈谈你在多年构建中意识到的最难的部分吗？比如你在这段旅程开始时可能甚至低估了什么？最难的技术部分是什么？

turns.en: I think the hard technical path is So one, right? Like you don't You have a lot of conviction and confidence in agents will use the web at scale. And a lot of it will Like you can A few of those things you can take to the bank and we had conviction. On the details, right? How fast will that happen? Which models? What will like I did not have the foresight to know that coding agents would be dominant in the way that they have been for a period, right? Like I would not have anticipated that. So now as you see these things unfold, you have to be agile around it while being opinionated about the long term. The second thing that's really hard is that you have to break to be in this business. You kind of have to break a bunch of roles, right? People will tell you so we are building a horizontal web business for a lot of customers that look very different from each other. We're telling the world that if you are buying models or LLMs using our search to enhance those tokens makes them more capable whether you're applying them for finance or legal or insurance underwriting or sales or recruiting or science or you come up with any use case for us, a human in a browser, which is basically everything, right? We are saying we are building a product that is useful across all of these modalities, right? So now these are very different kind of customers, very different kind of sales, very different kinds of value prop even in terms of the language you need to use. So building a really horizontal technology layer from day zero instead of ending up there by saying I'm going to go do a vertical and then gradually expand it is a different beast and you kind of have to break a lot of well-trodden startup building advice and pathways to go there and have that ambition.
turns.zh: 我认为困难的技术路径是，第一，对吧？比如你有很多信念和信心，认为智能体会大规模使用网络。其中很多你可以打包票，我们有信念。但细节上，对吧？那会多快发生？哪些模型？比如我没有先见之明知道编码智能体会像它们一段时间以来那样占据主导地位，对吧？比如我不会预料到。所以现在当你看到这些事情展开时，你必须灵活应对，同时对长期有主见。第二件真正困难的事是，要进入这个行业，你不得不打破很多角色，对吧？人们会告诉你，我们正在为许多彼此看起来非常不同的客户构建一个横向的网络业务。我们告诉世界，如果你购买模型或 LLM，使用我们的搜索来增强那些 token 会使它们更有能力，无论你将其应用于金融、法律、保险承保、销售、招聘、科学，或者你为我们想出任何用例，一个浏览器中的人类，这基本上就是一切，对吧？我们说我们正在构建一个在所有模态中都有用的产品，对吧？所以现在这些是非常不同的客户，非常不同的销售方式，非常不同的价值主张，甚至在你需要使用的语言方面。所以从第一天起就构建一个真正横向的技术层，而不是通过说我要先做一个垂直领域然后逐渐扩展来达到那里，是一种不同的野兽，你不得不打破许多老生常谈的创业建议和路径，才能到达那里并拥有那种雄心。

turns.en: And Google has the compute, the talent, the background, the index. Why isn't this Google's war to win? By a long distance.
turns.zh: 而谷歌有算力、人才、背景、索引。为什么这不是谷歌的战争，以很大优势获胜？

turns.en: I think you should invert the question.
turns.zh: 我认为你应该反过来问这个问题。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: Like make why would it be Google's war to win? As I said, the problem is entirely different. I think anytime there is such a rapid rate of change, my entire hypothesis of why I want it to be in a small thing is because a rapid rate of change favors a smaller agile thing. Um two I really think our goal, right? is to allow everyone's agent to be able to have access to the best search and all of the information on the web, right? Fundamentally, Google's goal is to allow it only for Google. If you are now running a open model on your hardware and you're running an agent there with your own inference, I want to provide it search. I want to provide it access to everything that anyone else could. And that is fundamentally not any of the larger, better capitalized people's goals, right? So in some sense, how we build our product, the pressures we feel, how we get feedback from the market is entirely different from how somebody else does. So then you can ask the question, do I get high fidelity, higher signal feedback? Do I attract better talent as a result of this strategy? There is a right level of, in my opinion, resources and resource constraint relative to the problem you want to solve. And in this case, I get to semi-orchestrate that to create the conditions for the best thing to get built, right? Like Google doesn't exercise any of these things or control. They're more forced to go with the flow while we get to create the perfect conditions for this to come into being.
turns.zh: 比如，为什么它会是谷歌的战争？正如我所说，问题完全不同。我认为任何时候有如此快速的变化率，我为什么希望它在一个小东西里的整个假设是因为快速变化有利于更小的敏捷的东西。第二，我真的认为我们的目标是让每个人的智能体都能访问最好的搜索和网络上的所有信息，对吧？从根本上说，谷歌的目标是只允许谷歌使用。如果你现在在硬件上运行一个开放模型，并在那里用自己的推理运行一个智能体，我想为它提供搜索。我想为它提供访问其他任何人都能访问的一切。而这从根本上不是任何更大的、资本更雄厚的人的目标，对吧？所以在某种意义上，我们如何构建产品、我们感受到的压力、我们如何从市场获得反馈，与其他人完全不同。所以你可以问，我是否获得了高保真、更高信号的反馈？我是否因此策略吸引了更好的人才？在我看来，相对于你想解决的问题，资源和资源约束有一个合适的水平。在这种情况下，我可以半编排这一点，为最好的东西被构建创造条件，对吧？比如谷歌不锻炼任何这些或控制。他们更多是被迫随波逐流，而我们可以为这件事的出现创造完美条件。

turns.en: So with Google on your first point also the Google point I agree they're big, stodgy, they also have their own not just bureaucracy but economy that they build. But the labs this is pretty critical infrastructure for the world they are building, you are building. Why wouldn't OpenAI and Anthropic want to own this? It's like central it's the world they are building and they are pretty agile and they are pretty execution oriented right now.
turns.zh: 所以关于谷歌，你的第一点，我也同意他们庞大、保守，他们不仅有官僚主义，还有他们建立的经济体系。但实验室——这对他们正在构建的世界、你正在构建的世界来说，是相当关键的基础设施。为什么 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 不想拥有这个？这就像中心，这是他们正在构建的世界，而且他们现在相当敏捷，相当注重执行。

turns.en: So one thing I said about Google still applies to labs right like when they build it they build it for their model.
turns.zh: 所以我说过的关于谷歌的一点仍然适用于实验室，对吧？当他们构建它时，他们是为他们的模型构建的。

turns.en: Yeah so it's model agnosticity.
turns.zh: 是的，所以是模型无关性。

turns.en: So that's one part of it, right? The other part is if you think about what is existential for them: it is the model, the layer above the model. And this is incident in my opinion—not because it's not important, right? Number two, the mission to democratize all information. It doesn't flow from AGI where you're saying your worldview, your world model, is: I will get a model which can do anything a human does, and I will make it so agile that it can deal with every bit, every tool that we have built for humans—as perfect or imperfect as that might be—and I will boil everything into this one thing, right? Our world model is that these things are going to be amazing and exist. But there are some tools like web search and the web where, instead of making the model good at adapting to this tool, you've got to adapt the tool because it's pervasive to the model. And I think sometimes that point of view and worldview collision, if you're right, gives you the edge. So now it boils down to: is our worldview right? And if our worldview is right, we will prevail.
turns.zh: 所以这是其中一部分，对吧？另一部分是，如果你想想对他们来说什么是存亡攸关的：是模型，是模型之上的那一层。而在我看来，这起事件——并不是因为它不重要，对吧？第二，让所有信息民主化的使命。它并非源于 AGI，那种你所说的世界观、你的世界模型是：我会得到一个能做任何人类能做的事的模型，我会让它如此灵活，以至于它能处理我们为人类构建的每一个工具——无论这些工具完美与否——并且我会把一切浓缩到这一个东西里，对吧？我们的世界模型是，这些东西将会非常惊人并存在。但有些工具，比如网络搜索和网络本身，与其让模型去适应这个工具，不如让工具去适应模型，因为它对模型来说是普遍存在的。我认为有时候，这种观点和世界观的碰撞，如果你是对的，就会给你优势。所以现在归结为：我们的世界观对吗？如果我们的世界观是对的，我们就会胜出。

turns.en: Your thesis relies on the internet remaining an open place. But there are big giants trying to be more walled gardens, right? Recently Amazon with, you know, Muse and Instinct is trying to be a walled garden. LinkedIn has always wanted to be a walled garden. We do a lot of recruiting here, so we know how much of a walled garden we actually use Parallel Web. So we are a customer. So do you feel if the large internet giants end up being walled gardens, that's a problem for Parallel? Or do you think at some point they are forced to flip? There's no way they can remain walled gardens in the world of agents.
turns.zh: 你的论点依赖于互联网保持开放。但有一些大巨头正试图变得更加封闭，对吧？最近亚马逊通过 Muse 和 Instinct 试图成为一个封闭花园。领英一直想成为一个封闭花园。我们在这里做很多招聘，所以我们知道我们实际上有多依赖 Parallel Web 这个封闭花园。所以我们是客户。那么你觉得，如果大型互联网巨头最终成为封闭花园，这对 Parallel 是个问题吗？还是你认为在某个时候他们会被迫转变？在智能体的世界里，他们不可能继续保持封闭花园。

turns.en: So actually I think it's perhaps even more interesting to talk about almost everyone in the web and their incentives. So there is a real risk, right? The web, the open web including many of these large players, is built on a few business models, right? What are the business models on the web? You have ads, you have subscriptions by the seat per human. You have e-commerce and transactions which could be for digital goods or physical goods, right? And then around transactions you have a mini affiliate economy or a payment economy or an economy around the payment flow, right? These are the core dominant business models. Now ads and subscriptions per human—it's very hard to imagine those surviving in their current form into a world that I imagine where agents are the primary consumers. Now e-commerce transactions, payment rails, perhaps even some affiliate stuff could survive and should—I imagine them surviving, right? Even there there is a real problem around broad-based matchmaking because previously you could have tolerated limiting your universe of what you would matchmake to based on committing to a merchant or something. But I think with agents that thing is going to get so efficient that you will exercise matchmaking and selection over the entire universe of availability. And so now we have to figure out how do we keep the web open because if we don't quickly build an incentive for people to have their content available to agents, invariably it's going to shut down. You're like, oh agents are stealing my stuff. I used to get paid by ads. I used to have people click through and buy subscriptions. Since people started using agents, anytime I put something out there for free, people steal it. I get nothing in return. Why should I keep doing this? Right? That's going to—and some very natural question, right? And I think that's part of what—I think the mission of the company is to keep the web open for agents, for everyone's agents. And not just—then you know, you shut it down for everyone and then you go to OpenAI or you go to Google or you go to some other large player and you're like, okay I'll give it to your agents if you pay me a bunch of money, and they do, and some content owners for a moment get paid, but then they stress about like, okay in two years this business—the agent business—is going to 50x, 30x, whatever. They're not going to pay me 30x.
turns.zh: 所以实际上，我认为谈论网络上几乎每个人及其激励措施可能更有趣。所以存在真实的风险，对吧？网络，包括许多这些大型参与者在内的开放网络，是建立在少数几种商业模式之上的，对吧？网络上的商业模式有哪些？有广告，有按人头订阅。有电子商务和交易，可能是数字商品或实物商品，对吧？然后在交易周围，有一个小型联盟经济或支付经济，或围绕支付流的经济，对吧？这些是核心主导的商业模式。现在，广告和按人头订阅——很难想象它们以当前形式存活在我所想象的智能体是主要消费者的世界里。现在，电子商务交易、支付轨道，也许甚至一些联盟 stuff 可以存活，也应该存活——我想象它们会存活，对吧？即使在那里，围绕广泛匹配也存在一个真正的问题，因为以前你可以容忍根据承诺给某个商家或其他东西来限制你匹配的宇宙。但我认为有了智能体，那件事将变得如此高效，以至于你将在整个可用性宇宙中行使匹配和选择。所以现在我们必须弄清楚如何保持网络开放，因为如果我们不迅速为人们建立激励，让他们的内容可供智能体使用，它不可避免地会关闭。你会说，哦，智能体在偷我的东西。我以前通过广告获得报酬。我以前有人点击并购买订阅。自从人们开始使用智能体，每当我把东西免费放在那里，人们就偷它。我什么也得不到。我为什么要继续这样做？对吧？那将会——这是一个非常自然的问题，对吧？我认为这是部分原因——我认为公司的使命是保持网络对智能体开放，对每个人的智能体开放。而不仅仅是——然后你知道，你对所有人关闭它，然后你去找 OpenAI 或谷歌或其他大型参与者，你说，好吧，我会把它给你的智能体，如果你付给我一大笔钱，他们付了，一些内容所有者暂时得到了报酬，但然后他们担心，好吧，两年后这个业务——智能体业务——将增长 50 倍、30 倍， whatever。他们不会付我 30 倍。

turns.en: But what's the incentive for them? I agree with everything you just said, but then there's a huge disincentive for LinkedIn, Amazon to go open, right?
turns.zh: 但他们的激励是什么？我同意你刚才说的一切，但然后领英、亚马逊有一个巨大的抑制因素去开放，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah. And so we have built this thing called Index where we have built a model to price every bit of content that an agent reads in terms of how much it helps the output. And I think that is now an interesting currency in town, right? You can usually for most places you can say, okay if I spent a little bit more compute on the problem, I get a marginally better answer. That's something we sort of intuitively now see in the data. We also believe it, right? Like, okay, if I use an Opus versus a Sonnet or a Haiku or an After versus a Soul or a Luna, I trust the results of the higher compute thing more because they empirically tend to get more things right and do them better, right? So now you're living in this world where when you do work and you produce output, you are saying if I spent a little bit more money on this, I could have gotten a marginally better output. Now I can trade that saying, okay, if I had access to your data as I did this work and it made my output marginally better or more desirable, oh, I could have done that with a dollar of compute. So you added a dollar of marginal value. Why would I spend compute when I could have paid you 75 cents on the dollar to get that data, not used up the GPUs? And so there is a bunch of data we have collected around this. We've trained models around this and we want to ultimately incentivize the creation of high quality content because models are not very useful if not given data and information, right? So you want them to have data. You want the people to have incentive to create the right and high quality data and make it accessible to everyone's agent and you want to do it at scale.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们构建了这个叫做 Index 的东西，我们构建了一个模型来为智能体阅读的每一点内容定价，定价依据是它对输出的帮助有多大。我认为这现在是城里一种有趣的货币，对吧？你通常可以在大多数地方说，好吧，如果我在问题上多花一点算力，我会得到一个稍微更好的答案。这是我们现在在数据中直观看到的东西。我们也相信它，对吧？比如，好吧，如果我使用 Opus 而不是 Sonnet 或 Haiku，或者 After 而不是 Soul 或 Luna，我更信任更高算力东西的结果，因为它们经验上倾向于做对更多事情并做得更好，对吧？所以现在你生活在这个世界里，当你做工作并产生输出时，你在说，如果我在这上面多花一点钱，我本可以得到稍微更好的输出。现在我可以交易那个说，好吧，如果我在做这项工作时能访问你的数据，它使我的输出稍微更好或更令人满意，哦，我本可以用一美元的算力做到那个。所以你增加了一美元的边际价值。为什么我要花算力，当我可以付你 75 美分 on the dollar 来获得那个数据，而不使用 GPU？所以我们收集了一堆关于这个的数据。我们围绕这个训练了模型，我们最终想要激励高质量内容的创作，因为模型如果没有数据和信息就不太有用，对吧？所以你想要它们有数据。你想要人们有激励去创造正确和高质量的数据，并使其可供每个人的智能体访问，并且你想大规模地做这件事。

turns.en: So this is almost like a new business, like advertising business model for the new internet.
turns.zh: 所以这几乎像是一个新业务，像是新互联网的广告商业模式。

turns.en: It's a version of—you can say, aspirationally, AdSense in its early days is what we think we can and should build here because otherwise you're going to have to pay some large lab or something rent to access this data and in the process you lose and the content owner loses.
turns.zh: 这是——你可以说，理想情况下，AdSense 早期就是我们认为我们可以并且应该在这里构建的东西，因为否则你将不得不付给某个大型实验室或其他东西租金来访问这些数据，在这个过程中你输，内容所有者输。

turns.en: What's been the reaction of the big guys to this, the walled gardens, I guess?
turns.zh: 大人物们对此的反应是什么，我猜是那些封闭花园？

turns.en: I think it's in flight. We have announced a collection of partnerships. We've not announced any partnerships with like a large walled garden as you describe it. But I think they feel and see the problem too. We've announced partnerships with some amazing partners like—I think we're working with like The Atlantic and Fortune if you think of like news publishers who have built real businesses over I don't know how long.
turns.zh: 我认为它正在进行中。我们已经宣布了一系列合作伙伴关系。我们还没有宣布与像你描述的大型封闭花园的任何合作伙伴关系。但我认为他们也感受到并看到了问题。我们已经宣布与一些了不起的合作伙伴的合作，比如——我认为我们正在与《大西洋月刊》和《财富》合作，如果你想想那些建立了真正业务的新闻出版商，我不知道多久了。

turns.en: We work with really interesting data providers across different verticals, like for VC. So you'll understand we work with PitchBook and Crunchbase. These are data sets which would otherwise be subscriptions by the seat. And we work with them to figure out when their data, with their authority and quality, produces marginally improved quality, how do we make sure we pay them? And increasingly we're expanding to a lot more of these content partners. But our ultimate goal is to have a super scalable business model that not just makes these businesses survive but thrive with real participation in the agent economy. And again, that only happens if the first premise I started with holds: agents will use the web 1000x more. So when you grow the pie a lot, you can use incentive alignment mechanics like the ones I'm proposing to actually incentivize everyone to collaborate.
turns.zh: 我们与不同垂直领域中非常有趣的数据提供商合作，比如风投领域。所以你会理解，我们与 PitchBook 和 Crunchbase 合作。这些数据集原本是按席位订阅的。我们与他们合作，弄清楚当他们的数据凭借其权威性和质量带来边际质量提升时，我们如何确保向他们付费？而且我们正越来越多地扩展到更多内容合作伙伴。但我们的最终目标是拥有一个超级可扩展的商业模式，不仅让这些企业生存下来，还能通过真正参与智能体经济而蓬勃发展。再说一次，这只有在我的第一个前提成立时才会发生：智能体将使用网络 1000 倍以上。所以当你把蛋糕做大很多时，你可以使用我提出的激励对齐机制来真正激励每个人合作。

transcript.secZh: 数据合作与智能体经济

transcript.sec: Future of the Internet and Agents

turns.en: I'm curious for your take on three, four years out—to the extent we can predict anymore. It's a crazy time to make any kind of predictions. What does the internet look like, or what does our world look like in three years? Do we only talk to agents, never go to a website really, other than maybe social media like Instagram?
turns.zh: 我很好奇你对三四年后的看法——在我们还能预测的范围内。现在做任何预测都是疯狂的时刻。三年后互联网会是什么样子，或者我们的世界会是什么样子？我们是否只与智能体交谈，除了像 Instagram 这样的社交媒体，真的再也不去网站了？

turns.en: Yeah, I think most of our interactions with the web as we think of it today will happen via agents. I think we continue to use experiences online. Those experiences perhaps don't really look like a traditional HTML website loading. They perhaps look a little bit more like an app, perhaps with more AI blended into it. But I think it would be rarish to go to the web to do work, right? So you'd go to the web for what I'd call experience or connection, some of these other needs. I think the biggest thing that to me feels again totally obvious about the future three, four years out is the predominant ways agents interact with the web won't just be the search or the pull, as I call it—like agents pulling information from the web—and will transform into a push, where your web system like Parallel will have enough context to know what you are interested in. You're kind of subscribed to a feed or a push stream which tells you, oh, this is what just changed in the world, which now requires your agent to do some computation to bring something to you, the person, or you, the company, right? So this transformation of the web from pull to push I think is what we start seeing. And I think until a few months ago, there were no agents which felt like they were always on and proactive. Now we are starting to see the very first set of agents which are creating this abstraction for you, an expectation for you that they are always on, they're proactive, and they're trying to know from your data and learn from their interactions with you what you might care about and go bring those to you proactively, right? I think if this plays out in the way I imagine, the web will have to change to go from this sort of pull to a push model. And that I think is what I'm really excited about. Like that is the singular thing that we think we will end up building.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为我们今天所想的与网络的大多数交互将通过智能体进行。我认为我们会继续使用在线体验。这些体验可能看起来不像传统的 HTML 网站加载。它们可能看起来更像一个应用，也许融入了更多 AI。但我认为去网上工作会很少见，对吧？所以你去网上是为了我所说的体验或连接，以及其他一些需求。我认为对我来说，未来三四年最明显的事情是，智能体与网络交互的主要方式将不仅仅是搜索或我所说的“拉取”——比如智能体从网络上拉取信息——而将转变为“推送”，你的网络系统如 Parallel 将有足够的上下文来知道你对什么感兴趣。你有点像订阅了一个信息流或推送流，它告诉你，哦，这是世界上刚刚发生变化的事情，现在需要你的智能体进行一些计算，把东西带给你这个人，或者你这家公司，对吧？所以我认为我们开始看到网络从拉取到推送的转变。而且我认为直到几个月前，还没有智能体感觉像是始终在线和主动的。现在我们开始看到第一批智能体，它们为你创造了这种抽象，对你有一种期望：它们始终在线、主动，并试图从你的数据中了解、从与你的交互中学习你可能关心什么，并主动把这些带给你，对吧？我认为如果这按照我想象的方式发展，网络将不得不从这种拉取模式转变为推送模式。而这正是我非常兴奋的。就像这是我们最终会构建的唯一东西。

transcript.secZh: 互联网与智能体的未来

transcript.sec: Google's Position in the New World

turns.en: Do you think Google is toast in this new world?
turns.zh: 你认为谷歌在这个新世界里完蛋了吗？

turns.en: So again, right? Like I think the word 'toast' is loaded. I think in this new world we are talking about such a potential expansion of the pie that you can simultaneously keep growing while losing share of market. In fact, share of market is a vague thing to define because the market itself is changing, right? So yeah, can Google—if you think of today the web search market, Google commands a hefty market share. Should and can Google command that market share of a future AI web search market? I would like to think no, obviously. But can they still grow their business even as this new market comes alive with its own set of events? Yes. So I think you can totally imagine a world where Google, with their accumulated capital, talent, technology, culture, momentum, distribution, continues to build an increasingly compelling business while new people like us create entirely new markets where we get to participate and play. And what we are betting on is like over time our market is bigger than their market.
turns.zh: 那么再说一次，对吧？我认为“完蛋”这个词带有倾向性。我认为在这个新世界里，我们谈论的是如此巨大的蛋糕扩张潜力，以至于你可以在失去市场份额的同时继续增长。事实上，市场份额是一个模糊的定义，因为市场本身在变化，对吧？所以是的，谷歌——如果你想想今天的网络搜索市场，谷歌拥有相当大的市场份额。谷歌应该且能够在一个未来的 AI 网络搜索市场中占据那样的市场份额吗？我显然认为不能。但即使这个新市场以其自身的一系列事件活跃起来，他们还能继续增长业务吗？是的。所以我认为你完全可以想象一个世界：谷歌凭借其积累的资本、人才、技术、文化、势头、分销渠道，继续打造越来越有吸引力的业务，而像我们这样的新人们创造全新的市场，我们参与其中并玩耍。而我们赌的是，随着时间的推移，我们的市场比他们的市场更大。

turns.en: Yeah, might have to go through a Microsoft-style transformation where, you know, under Satya Microsoft has gone through a transformation of product to services and GitHub and many other things drive it versus—
turns.zh: 是的，可能不得不经历一次微软式的转型，你知道，在萨提亚的领导下，微软经历了从产品到服务的转型，GitHub 和许多其他东西驱动它，而不是——

turns.en: I think this world is moving so fast that almost every business will have to undergo transformation. In fact, between now and four, five years from now I might have to go through two transformations myself, right? Like even as the new kid on the block—
turns.zh: 我认为这个世界发展得太快了，几乎每个企业都将不得不经历转型。事实上，从现在到四五年后，我自己可能就要经历两次转型，对吧？就像即使是作为新来的孩子——

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: —with a new potentially agile business like we like to think way more agile than anyone else we are talking about. In this market entirely premised on this wave we will still have to go through transformations.
turns.zh: ——带着一个可能敏捷的新业务，就像我们喜欢认为的比我们谈论的任何人都敏捷得多。在这个完全以这一波浪潮为前提的市场中，我们仍然必须经历转型。

turns.en: I want to shift gears towards your operating principles. First of all, how has being a startup CEO been similar and different to being Twitter CEO, public company, a large company? Maybe start with similarities.
turns.zh: 我想换个话题，谈谈你的运营原则。首先，作为初创公司 CEO 与作为 Twitter CEO、上市公司、大公司 CEO 有何异同？也许从相似之处开始。

turns.en: Today Parallel is getting bigger and on less—less than 120 maybe. And it is post product market fit on part of our business, right? So I think in the early days of Parallel it was very, very different. I think now you're starting to see some of the elements show up. But I think the common themes, right, are ultimately most leadership is about having followership, right? Like no matter what job you're in, if you're in what would be considered a leadership job or role, you're not going to be very effective unless you have your own brand or way of getting followership from people who can collectively do something special. That is at its premise common no matter what you are. So now the question is, can the same person be both? And I think we've seen time and again that even if the things that matter might be different, most entrepreneurs who end up scaling or doing multiple things prove that in different circumstances there are some common elements. And people have many different—there isn't one brand of leadership in the world. Each person builds their own way to find people, and people who end up finding the right people to collaborate with them at the right time end up doing interesting things. So those things are the same, right? I would say almost everything else is perhaps different, right? Like post product market fit, pre product market fit. Everyone cares what you do. No one cares what you do, right? Entirely technical hypothesis, there is no market, no customer. Like what do you do? How you recruit? Who you recruit? Everything is different.
turns.zh: 今天 Parallel 正在变大，大概不到 120 人。而且我们部分业务已经实现了产品市场契合，对吧？所以我认为在 Parallel 的早期，情况非常非常不同。我认为现在你开始看到一些元素显现出来。但我认为共同的主题，对吧，最终大多数领导力在于拥有追随者，对吧？就像无论你做什么工作，如果你处于被认为是领导职位或角色，除非你有自己的品牌或方式从能够共同做出特别事情的人那里获得追随，否则你不会很有效。这是无论你是什么的前提共同点。所以现在的问题是，同一个人能两者兼得吗？我认为我们一次又一次地看到，即使重要的事情可能不同，大多数最终扩大规模或做多件事的企业家证明，在不同情况下有一些共同元素。人们有许多不同的——世界上没有一种领导力品牌。每个人都建立自己的方式来寻找人，而那些最终在正确时间找到正确的人与他们合作的人最终会做出有趣的事情。所以那些事情是一样的，对吧？我会说几乎其他一切可能都不同，对吧？比如产品市场契合后、产品市场契合前。每个人都关心你做什么。没人关心你做什么，对吧？完全是技术假设，没有市场，没有客户。比如你做什么？你如何招聘？你招聘谁？一切都不同。

turns.en: What have you had to unlearn in your own behavioral styles as a leader to recruit, behave with your team in a technical problem versus a post product—yeah.
turns.zh: 作为领导者，在招聘、在技术问题中与团队相处的方式上，与产品市场契合后相比，你不得不摒弃哪些行为风格？是的。

turns.en: What's changed for you as a CEO?
turns.zh: 作为 CEO，你有哪些变化？

turns.en: I think the early days of Parallel were perhaps more natural for me, right? As the technical person among technical people, smart people, some deep conviction in something the world doesn't believe, building something that felt natural, in the zone. You don't think about learning or unlearning, right? You think about learning things, but in that sense those activities felt easy, natural. Like I wasn't sitting there like how do I unlearn things, right? What I do think is a common theme for how I work is I like doing—I think I'm only good and I only like jobs where I think that I am slightly unqualified for doing that. Right? Like when I took a software engineering job at Twitter after doing a PhD, because I felt like I was underqualified in that moment because I had done academic research, I had done prototypes—like real software engineering for real systems with real great engineers was a real challenge. As I took on every job at Twitter, I felt that someone was taking a bet on me in a way that me in my most rational moment should not, right? And so you only want jobs in my opinion that you feel slightly unqualified for because that drives, at least for me, all of the right behaviors, right? Like you are curious, you work that extra bit harder because you're not up to it. You aren't rinsing and repeating a thing. You are there with a curious open mind about like how do I go tackle this thing. You seek help from other people or from models. And so to me that is how I felt in every job at Twitter over time. Being a founder felt like that to me, right? Like I'm founding a thing I'm—
turns.zh: 我觉得 Parallel 的早期对我来说可能更自然，对吧？作为技术人员中的技术人员，聪明人中的聪明人，对某些世界不相信的事情有深深的信念，构建一些感觉自然、得心应手的东西。你不会去想学习或忘却，对吧？你会想学习东西，但在那种意义上，那些活动感觉轻松、自然。就像我没有坐在那里想我该如何忘却，对吧？我认为我工作的一个共同主题是我喜欢做——我认为我只擅长并且只喜欢那些我认为自己稍微不够格的工作。对吧？就像我在博士毕业后接受了 Twitter 的软件工程工作，因为我觉得当时自己不够格，因为我做过学术研究，做过原型——而真正的软件工程、为真实系统与真正优秀的工程师合作是一个真正的挑战。当我在 Twitter 承担每一项工作时，我都觉得有人在对我下注，而我在最理性的时刻都不应该下这样的注，对吧？所以在我看来，你只想要那些你觉得自己稍微不够格的工作，因为这会激发——至少对我来说——所有正确的行为，对吧？比如你会好奇，你会更努力一点，因为你能力不足。你不会重复做同样的事情。你带着好奇和开放的心态在那里思考我该如何解决这个问题。你向其他人或模型寻求帮助。所以对我来说，这就是我在 Twitter 每份工作中的感受。作为创始人对我来说也是那样，对吧？就像我在创立一个东西，我正在——

turns.en: Why are you unqualified for now?
turns.zh: 你现在为什么不够格？

turns.en: That is my current job. Entirely unqualified for like scaling the company. I'm like entirely unqualified for scaling an API business for developers and enterprises and growing at rapid scale a large team in a rapidly evolving world. Like I think anyone who thinks they have been trained for this hasn't been, right? Like I think these are—fortunate enough that we found ourselves in this unique moment in this unique position to go on this ride, but like I'm unqualified for almost everything I am supposed to be doing.
turns.zh: 那就是我现在的工作。完全不够格，比如扩张公司。我完全不够格去扩张一个面向开发者和企业的 API 业务，并在一个快速演变的世界中快速扩张一个大型团队。就像我认为任何认为自己受过训练的人其实都没有，对吧？我觉得这些是——我们足够幸运，发现自己处于这个独特的时刻、独特的位置，去经历这段旅程，但就像我几乎对我应该做的所有事情都不够格。

turns.en: As a CEO, how does your week actually look like? Do you have structure around it? Are you one of those who attacks different problems every week and there's not as much structure? Do you have weekly meetings?
turns.zh: 作为 CEO，你的一周实际上是什么样的？你对此有结构吗？你是那种每周处理不同问题、结构不太多的人吗？你有每周会议吗？

turns.en: It has evolved a lot. Things were very different about 6 months or a year ago when the team was materially smaller. Like the team has grown 4x this year—I want to say in like 9, 10 months—so it's a work in progress, the evolution of me. The core structure of the week that I care about the most is I like seeing engineering demos on Friday evenings. I don't know, it makes—like I like to see what is being built or what got built or what got shipped to connect it to some customer value that I really care about. I spend time on Mondays often with my leadership team. Mostly because every weekend is a new obsession or journey for me. Like Monday to Friday I think you're in the operational day-to-day. And every weekend you take like one step up and come up with what are we missing? What should I be paranoid about? Should we be going and creating a new area of the business? Do I need to go hire somebody with a special skill? Do I need to think about a customer differently or market differently? So every weekend you end up in—at least my usual goal is to select one obsession from three that are bubbling and try to come up with a conclusion by Monday morning, which is either this obsession is not something I should act on—which is the right answer half of the time—or this obsession seems worth pursuing, that I am going to hand something off to somebody to take it to the next level. And then I will figure out somewhere following up on it, right? So to me that is my cycle, a little bit around the weekend and the rest of the week. We have a company thing where we are in person in the office in a single office. And everyone is in the same office in product and engineering on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays in Palo Alto. People who live in San Francisco go to our San Francisco office on Tuesdays and Thursdays, right? So now my internal time with people I try to reserve as much of Monday, Wednesday, Friday as possible for that. External stuff to the extent possible I like to do on Tuesdays and Thursdays. So there's some natural cadence that gets built as a result, right? Um generally I don't like scheduled—almost no scheduled one-on-ones.
